newsitem.title: USA: Two Web sites linked to mass suicide group.
newsitem.headline: Two Web sites linked to mass suicide group.

text.p: A Web site linked to 39 people who committed mass suicide at a California mansion hails the comet Hale-Bopp as the herald of a spacecraft coming to "take us home to 'Their World' -- in the literal 'Heavens.'"

"We are happily prepared to leave 'this world' and go with Ti's crew," says the cryptic message on the Web site titled "Heaven's Gate -- How and When It May Be Entered." The message does not explain who or what Ti was.

News reports said the site on the globe-spanning Internet computer network was created by a member of Higher Source, an Internet services business that a Beverly Hill, California, businessmen said was run by the group.

Businessman Nick Matzorkis, who tipped police off to the deaths of the 39 men and women found on Wednesday at the mansion in Rancho Santa Fe near San Diego, said they killed themselves to rendezvous with a spacecraft they believed was hiding behind the comet.
Police on Thursday confirmed the deaths were caused by mass suicide.

Higher Source had a Web site touting its services but there was nothing to indicate a link with the group. The site, however, features numerous pictures of comets, stars and other astronomical phenomena -- as well as what looks like a spinning flying saucer.

Both Web pages could be viewed on Thursday by anyone in the world with a properly equipped computer and Internet access, although access became more difficult as news of the San Diego deaths spread. Heaven's Gate was accessible at http://www.heavensgate.com, while Higher Source was at http://207.155.252.4/(tilde)Font.

The "Heaven's Gate" home page -- a combination title page and table of contents -- contains links to other pages grouped in the site with mystifying names like "Our Position Against Suicide," "Last Chance To Advance Beyond Human," and "How a Member of the Kingdom of Heaven Might Appear."
But the page's most striking feature is its introductory message welcoming the recently visible Hale-Bopp, one of the brightest comets to appear in the sky in recent memory.
"Red Alert ... HALE-BOPP Brings Closure," say the site's opening words.
"Whether Hale-Bopp has a 'companion' or not is irrelevant from our perspective," the page says. "However, its arrival is joyously very significant to us at 'Heaven's Gate.'

"The joy is that our Older Member in the Evolutionary Level Above Human (the 'Kingdom of Heaven') has made it clear to us that Hale-Bopp's approach is the 'marker" we've been waiting for -- the time for the arrival of the spacecraft from the Level Above Human to take us home to 'Their World' -- in the literal Heavens.
"Our 22 years of classroom here on planet Earth is finally coming to conclusion --'graduation' from the Human Evolutionary Level," the message says.

"... If you study the material on this website you will hopefully understand our joy and what our purpose here on Earth has been. You may even find your 'boarding pass' to leave with us during this brief 'window,'" it says.
The page also offers the opportunity to order two videotapes, including one titled "Planet Earth About To Be Recycled -- Your Only Chance To Survive -- Leave With Us."
The videotapes and a book advertised as an anthology of the group's materials can be ordered via electronic mail or from a company called Telah Services in Phoenix, the site says.

The Web -- information on the Internet enlivened by pictures, sound and video -- may not have been the only place on the Net that Heaven's Gate was active. The Internet news service Wired News reported that someone for months had been posting a message similar to the one on the Web page on the Net discussion groups known as newsgroups.

Higher Source's Web site was much more conventional in comparison to Heaven's Gate's. The site offers Web site design services, Internet security services, computer programming, computer network services and digital telephone work.
Matzorkis, who runs a computer company in Beverly Hills, California, called Interact Entertainment, said he had dealings with the group, which he said was called "WW Higher Source."
He said he had contracted some Web site designs to the group and had communicated with 15 or 16 of its members, who referred to themselves as "monks."
